What We Learned

  1. Remove the expected linear part. When a functional equation suggests an affine solution, defining an auxiliary function such as can isolate the remaining structure.

  2. Compare substitutions with the same composed argument.
    Choosing two pairs with the same value of makes the terms involving comparable. Here this turns the functional equation into a first-order recurrence.

  3. Injectivity and non-injectivity provide different anchors.
    Injectivity controls values in the image of , whereas non-injectivity produces two distinct inputs with the same output. After that, the two cases can be handled by parallel recurrence arguments.

  4. A constant finite difference is highly restrictive on . Once a recurrence of the form is obtained, equality at two distinct indices can force that constant to vanish.
